title: WebMCP Demo — a live map for thinking with your own agent
pitch: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan.
about_excerpt: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan. Like Comment Story Updates The live map: your own ChatGPT asks questions, clears "don't know" marks, and turns branches into checkable tasks — via 6 WebMCP tools. What it does Most WebMCP demos let an agent operate a site's transactional surface — fill a form, add to cart. This project inverts that: the page is a blank thinking canvas, and the tools it publishes are generative . You put down one thing you want to figure out ("I want to buy my first home"), and your own ChatGPT — with your context and memory — thinks with you on the map: It starts by asking questions as nodes , not by dumping a plan. You answer by growing branches yourself ; every edit you make on the canvas is delivered to the agent on its next tool call. Mark anything with "Don't know" and your confusion literally becomes the agenda — the agent clears those marks first, with concrete first steps. Steps become checkable task nodes , a Plan view folds the map into goal / premises / next tasks, and checking a task off in either place updates both. The page runs no AI of its own . It publishes six WebMCP tools; the visitor brings the intelligence. Thoughtful use of WebMCP The interesting problems turned out to be protocol-level, and we solved them in ways any WebMCP app can reuse: Read-before-write, enforced server-side. read_map returns a state token; every write requires it. A stale or missing token gets a 409 whose error text steers the agent back to read_map . The guard doubles as optimistic locking between the human and the agent. Human actions as first-class input. Everything the human does on the canvas (add, edit, move, delete, mark, check) is queued and delivered inside the next tool result — with a consuming read reserved for the agent and a non-consuming variant ( ?deliver=0 ) for the page's own refreshes, so the UI can never starve the agent of events. Granularity enforced by schema, not prose. add_nodes accepts at most 3 nodes per call (schema + server both), because a map that fills up in one shot stops feeling like a conversation. A capability split that matches the relationship. Agents can add, annotate, resolve, remove, and bulk-arrange — but the layout engine owns placement, and destructive actions on human-placed nodes are steered to require conversation first. Robust registration in the real world. Tools register before app mount, tolerate late injection of navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext (ChatGPT's browser and Chrome differ), and the footer shows live tool status for devtools-less in-app browsers. Why it matters "I know what I want, but not the way there" is a universal state — buying a home, relocating, incorporating, a first tax return. Chat alone answers and scrolls away; to-do apps assume you already know the steps. A shared, persistent map that your own agent can touch bridges the two: the conversation leaves a structure, and the structure becomes a plan you can execute and check off. Because the page hosts no model and pays no inference cost, this pattern is adoptable by any site: publish tools, let visitors bring their agents. How we built it Go + Postgres single-origin service (API, SSE live updates, static React/TypeScript SPA) on Render. The canvas is Miro-like: pan/zoom, drag, click-to-grow, right-click menu. A height-aware tidy-tree layout engine keeps the map clean after every structural change, verified against real DOM rects. WebMCP tool descriptions live in one file — they were the main behavior-tuning surface, iterated against the real ChatGPT desktop browser. What's next Multiple maps as a shelf, session-to-session continuity ("continue from where the fog cleared last week"), and the same canvas working with other WebMCP-capable agents out of the box.
